name: Mentors
description: In BerSoft $$$n$$$ programmers work, the programmer $$$i$$$ is characterized by a skill $$$r_i$$$. A programmer $$$a$$$ can be a mentor of a programmer $$$b$$$ if and only if the skill of the programmer $$$a$$$ is strictly greater than the skill of the programmer $$$b$$$ $$$(r_a \gt r_b)$$$ and programmers $$$a$$$ and $$$b$$$ are not in a quarrel. You are given the skills of each programmers and a list of $$$k$$$ pairs of the programmers, which are in a quarrel (pairs are unordered). For each programmer $$$i$$$, find the number of programmers, for which the programmer $$$i$$$ can be a mentor.
input_specification: The first line contains two integers $$$n$$$ and $$$k$$$ $$$(2 \le n \le 2 \cdot 10^5$$$, $$$0 \le k \le \min(2 \cdot 10^5, \frac{n \cdot (n - 1)}{2}))$$$ — total number of programmers and number of pairs of programmers which are in a quarrel. The second line contains a sequence of integers $$$r_1, r_2, \dots, r_n$$$ $$$(1 \le r_i \le 10^{9})$$$, where $$$r_i$$$ equals to the skill of the $$$i$$$-th programmer. Each of the following $$$k$$$ lines contains two distinct integers $$$x$$$, $$$y$$$ $$$(1 \le x, y \le n$$$, $$$x \ne y)$$$ — pair of programmers in a quarrel. The pairs are unordered, it means that if $$$x$$$ is in a quarrel with $$$y$$$ then $$$y$$$ is in a quarrel with $$$x$$$. Guaranteed, that for each pair $$$(x, y)$$$ there are no other pairs $$$(x, y)$$$ and $$$(y, x)$$$ in the input.
output_specification: Print $$$n$$$ integers, the $$$i$$$-th number should be equal to the number of programmers, for which the $$$i$$$-th programmer can be a mentor. Programmers are numbered in the same order that their skills are given in the input.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 978F — Mentors [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
